title: 100 Percent
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane unpacks the popular but vague Doug Lemov-derived classroom-management advice to "insist on 100 percent" compliance, arguing teachers who treat it as a blunt rule crash and burn because the real insight is narrower: anything less than 100 percent risks a slippery slope from 90 to 80 to 50 percent, not that every instruction must be enforced to the letter every time. He walks through escalating tactics for compliance short of a power struggle -- a quiet reminder paired with a stated reason, individual follow-up conversations to understand what's actually going on with a non-complying student, and a full-class reset with restated reasoning only when the number of non-compliant students is too large for individual check-ins. Kane is emphatic that public power struggles are the single biggest mistake teachers make with this advice, since publicly coercing a student erodes the relationship if they comply and broadcasts the conflict to the whole class if they don't, and either outcome raises fairness questions about whether the same standard applies to every student every time. His second major point is selectivity: teachers should pick a small number of things -- for Kane, silence during directions and mini-whiteboard participation -- to actually hold at 100 percent, rather than fighting every minor compliance issue, since consistency is more achievable and more valuable across a few chosen priorities than across everything. He closes by generalizing the same principle to helping confused students: solve it one-on-one rather than in a long public exchange that can embarrass the student and discourage others from admitting confusion.
points: Kane reframes \"insist on 100 percent\" as really meaning \"beware the slippery slope\" -- the danger isn't one instance below 100 percent, it's the drift from 90 to 80 to 50 percent that follows if it's tolerated.

His escalation ladder for non-compliance runs from a quiet reminder with a stated reason, to individual follow-up conversations, to a full-class reset -- with public power struggles explicitly identified as the single biggest mistake teachers make.

Kane argues selectivity matters as much as insistence: he holds only silence-during-directions and mini-whiteboard participation to a true 100 percent standard, rather than fighting every minor compliance issue in the room.
He extends the same principle to academic confusion, arguing a long public exchange to help one confused student humiliates them and teaches the rest of the class that admitting confusion isn't safe.
quotes: If you accept less than 100 percent, you risk a slippery slope. First it's 90 percent, then it's 80 percent, then it's 50 percent.
It's not \"insist on 100 percent every time,\" it's \"beware the slippery slope.\
The most important thing is not to get into a power struggle in front of the class. This is where the 100 percent advice leads a lot of teachers astray.
Even if the student listens you have eroded your relationship with that student by publicly humiliating them. If the student doesn't listen you have broadcasted the conflict to the entire class.
Less is more: pick a few things you care about and do them well, especially when you’re new.
But getting into a long conversation in front of everyone can be embarrassing, and convince other kids it’s not worth speaking up when you’re confused.
